name: 奈良 オモテナシ食堂 (Nara Omotenashi Shokudo)

claims.text: Offers a clearly meat-free vegetable plate with around 350g of vegetables across roughly eight dishes, making it an easy choice for diners avoiding meat.

name: 寧楽料理 こくとぅーら (Nara Ryori Coctura)

claims.text: The cooking is explicitly built on dashi, soy sauce and miso as its Japanese seasoning base, all of which typically contain or accompany wheat.

name: 奈良町 あしびの郷 (Naramachi Ashibi-no-Sato)

claims.text: The kitchen serves wheat-flour udon and miso-marinated fish in the same set meals, so cross-contact with wheat is likely; no gluten-free protocol is documented.
Set meals rely on miso and pickle seasonings; narazuke and Japanese miso/soy seasonings typically contain wheat. No wheat-free seasoning is documented.
Pickle and vegetable dishes are plated alongside grilled fish and fish-dashi soups in the standard sets, so vegan diners cannot assume separation.
The menu is built around pickled Yamato vegetables and Nara-grown rice, so vegetable-forward, lighter options are available even if not certified vegan or gluten-free.

name: ならまち分校スイーツ部 (Naramachi Bunko Sweets-bu)

claims.text: Desserts are built on dairy (milk syrups, matcha cream/espuma, soft serve) and the kitchen also makes crepes and galettes, so plant-based requests cannot be reliably accommodated.

name: ならまち 招福庵 (Naramachi Shofukuan)

claims.text: Core offerings are built on naturally fermented, plant-forward ingredients — rice-koji amazake, fermented red-bean anko, and Yamato-tea matcha — several of which are inherently free of wheat and animal products.

name: ならまち 鮨 はなこ (Naramachi Sushi Hanako)

claims.text: Nigiri are pre-seasoned and served with nikiri soy sauce; standard soy sauce is brewed with wheat, making this unsuitable for strict gluten avoidance.

name: 日本料理かがりや（篝屋） (Nihon Ryori Kagariya)

claims.text: Menu includes wheat-based Miwa somen noodles and soy sauce, and traditional kaiseki preparation relies on shared dashi and sauces, so cross-contact with gluten is likely; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Courses feature traditional soy sauce ('ancient soy sauce'), which is standard wheat-fermented Japanese shoyu unless otherwise specified.

This is a meat- and fish-forward kaiseki kitchen with signature courses built on Yamato beef, chicken, pork and duck, and dashi (fish stock) is standard in seasoned and simmered dishes, so vegan cross-contact is likely.
Seasonal vegetable-focused sets featuring Nara-grown produce are available, giving non-strict diners some plant-forward options.

name: 日本料理 滴翠 (Nihon Ryori Tekisui)

claims.text: The hotel asks guests to inform them of any allergies or food preferences at the time of reservation.
